subsubsection.title: Introduction
subsubsection.p: Trigonometry, Math123 is designed to give you tools to succeed in various programs in science, such as health professions, geology, and biology.

subsubsection.title: Course Description

blockquote.p: Math123 is a study of oscillatory behavior, circular functions, and their applications. In order to understand these things, it is important to see where they arise. This means analyzing data or situations, choosing among appropriate models, and solving applied problems. Of course, we can't predict every situation you will encounter in your future, so it is also important to develop flexibility and resilience.

subsubsection.p: More information can be found in and .

subsubsection.title: Learning is fun!
subsubsection.p: Learning is about feeding our curiosity, stretching ourselves to be better, finding out, and understanding. Those things are all rewarding, which is another word for fun. When learning isn't fun, there is something badly wrong.
You know what isn't fun? Grades. Getting them, assigning them, working for them none of these things are fun. They are, in many ways, the opposite of fun.

A growing body of evidence shows essentially no correlation between grades and success in future endeavors. Anecdotal evidence and educational research support the idea that grades, in fact, create a dis-incentive for learning and create incentives for several negative behaviors, including engaging in academic dishonesty (cheating). Neuroscience research further shows that dopamine is critical for learning, except in the case of learning with punishment. In other words, you need fun to learn. See, for example,
One thing we will do in this course is remove the pressure of the grade using a version of specifications grading that is sometimes called ungrading. More details are in .

subsubsection.title: Math is fun!
subsubsection.p: Many of you may have an experience of mathematics that does not suggest math is fun. Even if you know and appreciate the usefulness of math, the subject is often presented in a way that sucks all the fun out of it. Imagine sitting down to play a video game and finding that before you can actually start playing the game, you must first spend hours and hours memorizing cheat codes! Now we need to master the up, up, down, down, left, right, left, right, B, A, Start sequence and its variations. This will make later games easier. Enter this sequence 35 times on the next screen.

This is nothing like what mathematics really is. Yes, sometimes memorizing techniques can make later things easier, but these techniques have deeper meanings and origins. They are not just a random sequence of buttons to push.

Instead, mathematics is about analyzing situations, carefully describing or quantifying them, and looking for (more or less universal) patterns. That may still sound dry, but my personal goal in this class, in addition to giving you useful techniques, is to help you to see the beauty and joy of mathematics.

subsubsection.title: Additional Content
subsubsection.p: In addition to developing mathematical tools, techniques, and skills, we will seek to further our understanding of the role and importance of mathematics as a not only a tool, but as a field of human endeavor. We will explore how various concepts have developed and evolved, and how various mathematical models are interrelated.

subsection.title: Introduction to Ungrading
subsection.p: As mentioned earlier, substantial evidence shows that grades and grading are inherently antithetical to learning. Ungrading shifts the goal of a course from achievement to learning.

It is also important to note that the content of this course focuses on developing conceptual and procedural fluency with a set of concepts and tools as well as developing a mathematical mindset. Thus, it makes sense to have learning targets that students need to satisfy in order to consider the course successful.

Ultimately, though, this is your course. It is you who are the learner, and so you are in the best position to determine what will be of the most interest, what will be the most engaging, and, beyond the basics, what will be of the most value to you. More than that, you are the best person to determine how much you have learned. Therefore, you will be an active participant in determining the direction of the course and in your evaluation.

To put things bluntly, I will determine, based on a set of learning targets and a body of evidence that you present to me, whether you have done the work necessary to pass the class. Beyond that, you will determine your own grade, based on the evidence you present that you have met your own goals, as outlined in .

subsection.title: Portfolio and Reader's Guide
subsection.p: During the first week of class, we will discuss as a class what success in this class might look like, and then you will meet individually with me to develop a set of personalized goals. (See .)
These goals will not about grades and grading. Instead, you are invited to consider your learning, and more generally what success in this course will be for you.

Over the course of the semester, you will assemble a comprehensive portfolio that demonstrates that you have met the basic requirements for the course and demonstrates your progress toward your goals. Part of this portfolio will be three Progress Checks.

In addition to the Progress Checks, you are expected to regularly submit items to me for focused feedback. Based on this feedback, you will reflect, rework, extend, and revise as necessary to meet basic requirements and show forward progress.
At least one time, mid-semester, you will schedule an individual meeting to discuss your progress, your successes, and any challenges you are facing.

For each individual meeting, you will prepare and share with me an agenda or guide ahead of time with specific items you wish to discuss. This guide should discuss successes, challenges, and progress, and should direct the reader where to find evidence of these items. For example, you might include something along the lines of Successes Since our last meeting, I have reviewed and improved my understanding of difference quotients and average rate of change. Some good examples of my understanding and interpretation can be found in Driving North/South and Filling a Tank.These titles are completely invented and may not be anything like the titles of activities we actually use.

Your guide should also address the following questions.
What are you particularly proud of or excited about?
What has been challenging?
What do you plan to do next?, and
What do you need from me (the instructor) to facilitate your progress toward your goals?

For your final portfolio conference, which will be during the week of final exams, you will submit your final portfolio (with a final version of your reader's guide), again citing items of interest. Then, based on your learning and progress toward your goals and your submitted evidence, you will tell me what grade you have earned for the course.

introduction.p: This course is subject to the GVSU policies listed at . The following policies also apply.

Use of Generative AI Large Language Models [LLMs] (such as ChatGPT, Gemini, Copilot, etc.) in this class is subject to a few conditions, namely , , and . Transparency and accountability are fairly straight-forward, and are closely related to , but awareness is both more subtle and arguably more important.

subsubsection.title: Awareness
subsubsection.p: If you plan to use generative AI in this class, be aware of what you are using it for and whether it helps you toward your goals or just wastes your time. I find a useful analogy to be the idea of taking a forklift to the gym.

If your goal in going to the gym is to strengthen your muscles by lifting weights, using a forklift to lift the weights defeats the purpose. Sure, you can get in your reps, you can lift more than you could without the forklift, and you can do more reps and not get tired, but it doesn't work toward your goal of strengthening your muscles. It is a waste of your time. Worse, it gets in other people's way as they try to reach their strength training goals.

On the other hand, maybe you went to the gym because you work there and the boss wants you to move several large, heavy machines from one part of the building to another. If that's the case, using the forklift makes a lot of sense, because it is in fact helping with your goal of moving the machines.
Education is about strengthening your mental muscles. Be aware of how the use of heavy machinery either helps or hinders your progress.

Awareness also includes awareness of the ethical and practical pitfalls involved in using generative AI. You should be aware that
AI is trained on the works of other people
Plausibility, not objective truth, is the training goal of AI. It often makes things up that sound plausible.
AI is resource intensive. For example, according to , a paragraph of AI generated text uses more than 23 times as much electricity and water than a Google search without AI.

subsubsection.title: Transparency
subsubsection.p: When you use generative AI, be transparent: make note of exactly what you asked the AI to do (your prompts), and exactly what part of the AI results you used in your materials. For example, you might include something like the following in your portfolio.

p.q: In this problem, we were asked to model the number of hours of daylight as a function of the date. I knew this would be either sine or cosine, but I still didn't understand how to make the right days line up with the peaks and valleys, so I asked Copilot to explain. My prompt was Explain how to shift a sine function so that the peaks and valleys line up with data.

Copilot started by giving a formula for a sine function as y=A\sin\big(B(x-C)\big)+D and then gave step-by-step alignment guide. The important part for me was how to adjust the phase shift, C. It said to Find where a peak (or valley) occurs in your data, and shift the sine wave so its peak matches that point: C = x\text{-value of desired peak}. I was then able to align the peak amount of sunlight with June 21 by using C=172 days since the beginning of the year.

subsubsection.title: Accountability
subsubsection.p: When you use generative AI, you are accountable. What that means is that you must be able to explain all of your work and understand the power and the limitations of using LLMs.

Using the example of fitting a sine wave, a student submitting this should have noticed that Copilot got it wrong. Setting C=172 places the midline of the sine function at x=172 days. Using C=172 in the formula y=A\cos\big(B(x-C)\big)+D would place the peak at x=172, or you could find the date of the spring equinox and set C to that value in y=A\sin\big(B(x-C)\big)+D.

subsection.title: Time Management
subsection.p: One of my goals for this course is to challenge you to grow intellectually while giving you the tools and environment that will allow you to succeed. If you at any time feel that you are not being challenged to achieve your fullest potential in understanding the concepts we address, or if you have comments about the pace of the class or any other concerns, I encourage you to discuss your concerns with me during my student hours or an appointment with me.

As a university mathematics course, you should expect the course to be challenging. While we will all work to make time spent in class as productive as possible, it is not possible to learn everything using class time alone: much of your learning and understanding will occur as you reflect on what we have done in class, work on problems, and read and discuss course material outside of class.

The most important rule for this course is do not get behind in your work. Using a portfolio removes the inherent penalties in a slow start, but the trade off is that it can be tempting to put things off until later. Always stay up to date with the material in this course. Make succeeding in this course a priority!

subsubsection.title: Main Ideas
subsubsection.p:
The main take-away ideas from the introduction to vectors were:
Vectors describe quantities that have not only a magnitude, or size, but also a direction.
Vectors are often represented graphically using arrows, with a tail, where the vector starts, and a head, where the vector ends.
A vector can be interpreted as a change, and graphically, only the direction and size, not the specific location, of a vector is important. So, for example, an arrow from (0,0) to (30, -60) and an arrow from (-10,30) to (20,-30) are different representation of the exact same vector, because in each case the x-coordinate changes by +30 and the y-coordinate changes by -60.
Two ways to represent vectors algebraically are using angle brackets, such as \Avec{30,-60}, with the elements of the vector listed horizontally, and using square brackets, such as \left[\begin{array}{r}30\\-60\end{array}\right], with the elements listed vertically.
Because the angle bracket and square bracket representations of vectors take a lot of space, we will often name vectors by assigning them to a variable, usually written either as a bold letter or an italic letter with an arrow over it. So, we might say something like let \vec{v}=\Avec{30,-60} and let \vec{w}=\Avec{20,20}.
Vectors can be combined by adding them. Writing \vec{u}=\vec{v}+\vec{w} indicates that if we add \vec{v} and \vec{w} the resultant vector is \vec{u}. Graphically, to find \vec{u}=\vec{v}+\vec{w} when we are given \vec{v} and \vec{w}, we place the tail of \vec{w} at the head of \vec{v}, and \vec{u} is the vector from the tail of \vec{v} to the head of \vec{w}. (See example below.)

example.title: Addition of Vectors
example.p: Let \vec{v}=\Avec{30,-60} and let \vec{w}=\Avec{20,20}. Let \vec{u}=\vec{v}+\vec{w}. We will represent the addition of \vec{v} and \vec{w} graphically and algebraically.

To add \vec{v} and \vec{w} graphically, since we have no information about where the tail of \vec{v} should go, we will draw \vec{v} with its tail at the origin (and so its head is at (30,-60)). Then, we draw \vec{w} with its tail at the head of \vec{v}. Then, the vector \vec{u}=\vec{v}+\vec{w} will have its tail at the tail of \vec{v} and its head at the head of \vec{w}. So, for this example, the tail of \vec{u} is at the origin and the head of \vec{u} is at (50,-40). Note: We have included a grid and tick marks on the graph, but they are not necessary. You can add vectors graphically without knowing their algebraic values!

subsubsection.title: Extensions
subsubsection.p: While we have looked at vectors in two dimensions, in the xy-plane, there are also three dimensional vectors that behave in pretty much the exact same way! Depending on how the semester goes, we may briefly take a look at three-dimensional vectors.

There are lots of things that can be treated as vectors. Mathematicians define what it means to be a vector not so much in terms of what something is, but more in terms of how it behaves, but we won't get that in this class.

Another thing to be aware of is that sometimes we want to graphically add vectors that are not drawn tail-to-head. For example, we might wish to add two vectors that are currently drawn with their tails in the same place. (This is common for forces acting on a body in physics applications.)

worksheet.title: Height of a Ferris Wheel Car

introduction.p: shows the height of a Ferris wheel car as a function of the distance the car has travelled from the bottom. A full animation is available from the National Council of Teachers of Mathematics [NCTM] Illuminations classroom resources, Investigating Functions with a Ferris Wheel: Distance vs. Height ().

figure.caption: Height of a Ferris Wheel Car

introduction.p: For the calculations in this exercise, assume that the circumference of the Ferris wheel is 128m, and recall that the circumference, C, of a circle is given by C=2\pi{}r, where r is the radius of the circle.
We will refer to the height as h and the distance travelled as d.

statement.p: Find the total height of the Ferris wheel (in meters).

solution.p: The total height is twice the radius. Since the radius is \frac{128\text{m}}{2\pi}, the total height is \frac{128\text{m}}{\pi}\approx 40.74367m.

statement.p: When d=32m, find the value of h. That is, when the car when has travelled 32m, how high is it?

solution.p: When the car has travelled 32m, it has travelled one quarter of the way around, or half-way to the top. Thus its height is half the total height, approximately 20.37183m.

statement.p: Find h when d=64m.

solution.p: When the car has travelled 64m, it has travelled half of the way around, so it is at the top. Thus its height is the same as the total height, approximately 40.7467m.

statement.p: How much distance along the circle has the cab traversed at the moment it first reaches a height of \frac{128\text{m}}{2\pi}\approx 20.37183m?

solution.p: We know that \frac{128\text{m}}{2\pi} is the radius, which is also half the diameter, and so the height is half of the total height. The first time the car reaches this height is when it has travelled \frac{1}{4} of the way around, which is \frac{128\text{m}}{4}=32m.

statement.p: How much distance along the circle has the cab traversed at the moment it reaches a height of \frac{128\text{m}}{2\pi}\approx 20.37183m for the second time?

solution.p: The second time the car reaches a height of is when it has travelled \frac{3}{4} of the way around, which is \frac{3}{4}128\text{m}=96m.

statement.p: Can we express h as a function of d?

solution.p: Every distance travelled corresponds to exactly one position on the circular path of the Ferris wheel car, and each position has a particular height. Since there is always exactly one value of h for each value of d, we can express h as a function of d.

statement.p: Can we express d as a function of h?

solution.p: As the Ferris wheel car travels around its circular path, it passes through each height multiple times. Since there is not always exactly one value of d for each value of h, we cannot express d as a function of h.

worksheet.p: An important idea in setting up mathematical models that is often assumed or overlooked is the fact that you get to choose where you measure from. Sometimes the choice of your referece point is the difference between straight-forward calculations and much more complicated ones. With that in mind, we will revisit the Ferris wheel problem, but with a couple of slight twists.

First, instead of measuring height above the ground, we will measure the height, h, as the vertical distance from a horizontal line through the center of the Ferris wheel. Of course, we will need to indicate whether a given height is above the center or below the center, so we will use positive values of h to indicate distance above the center line, and negative values to indicate distance below the center line.
Second, we will measure the distance the Ferris wheel car has travelled relative to the point where it is farthest to the right. In other words, when it is on the center line.
Here, distances that are before reaching the line will be negative, and distances after will be positive.

introduction.p: For this problem, we will consider a Ferris wheel whose total height is 40m.

Recall that we are measuring distance travelled, d, relative to the point on the circle to the extreme right, and we are measuring the height, h, relative to the center of the Ferris wheel, so, for example, when d=0m, h=0m.

statement.p: How high is the center of the Ferris wheel above the ground?

solution.p: The total height is 40m, so the center is half that distance above the ground, which is 20m.

statement.p: What is the circumference of the Ferris wheel?

solution.p: We will call the radius of the Ferris wheel r and the circumference C. Since the total height is twice the radius, we have r=20m, and thus C=2\pi r=2\pi\cdot 20\text{m}\approx{}125.6637m.

statement.p: What is the value of h when 31.4159m?

solution.p: When the car has travelled 31.4159\text{m}=\frac{1}{4}\cdot{}125.6637m, it has travelled \frac{1}{4} of the circumference. Because we are measuring d from the point on the extreme right, this means that the Ferris wheel car is at its highest point. Since we are measuring h from the center of the Ferris wheel, that means that h=20m.

statement.p: What is the value of h when d=62.8315m?

solution.p: When the car has travelled 62.8315\text{m}=\frac{1}{2}\cdot{}125.6637m, it has travelled \frac{1}{2} of the circumference. Because we are measuring d from the point on the extreme right, this means that the Ferris wheel car is at the extreme left. Since we are measuring h from the center of the Ferris wheel and we are back at the original height, that means that h=0m.

statement.p: What is the value of h when d=94.2478m?

solution.p: When the car has travelled 94.2478\text{m}=\frac{3}{4}\cdot{}125.6637m, it has travelled \frac{3}{4} of the circumference. Because we are measuring d from the point on the extreme right, this means that the Ferris wheel car is at the bottom of its path, so it is 20m below the center, and therefore h=-20m.

worksheet.title: Distance and Angles

introduction.p: In , we know that the Ferris wheel is 40m tall, so it has a radius of 20m. We also know that the circumference is C=2\pi{}r\approx{}125.6637m. Said another way, the radius would fit 2\pi\approx6.28 times around the circle. Given two points on a circle, the part of the circle between them is called an arc, and its length is, appropriately, called the arc length. So, there are 2\pi radii of arc length in a circle.

It's not too much of a stretch to wonder how many radii of arc length lie between two points on a circle, and in fact, it gives a very natural way to measure angles, because given any angle, the arc length determined by the angle depends on the radius of the circle, and if an angle has an arc length of one radius on one circle, that same angle has one radius of arc length on any circle!

figure.caption: One radius of arc length on two different circles

description.p: One radius of arc length on two circles of different radius with the same center.

introduction.p: An angle that has one radius of arc length has a measure of1radian. Both of the angles shown in , \angle{}AOB and \angle{}aOb, have a measure of1radian, which we will often abbreviate as 1\text{ rad}.
In this problem, we again consider a circle (a Ferris wheel) with a radius of20m.

statement.p: When the car has travelled through1rad of angle, how much distance (arc length) has it travelled?

solution.p: When the car has travelled one radian, it has travelled a distance (arc length) equal to its radius. Since the radius is 20m, the car has travelled 20m.

statement.p: When the car has travelled through an angle of 2.5rad, how much arc length has it travelled?

solution.p: When the car has travelled 2.5rad, it has travelled an arc length that is 2.5 times its radius, so it has travelled an arc length of 2.5\cdot20\text{m}=50m.

statement.p: When the car has travelled through 30m of arc length, what angle (in radians) has it travelled through?

solution.p: When when the car has travelled through \thetarad, it has travelled a distance of \theta\cdot 20m, so we can solve 20\text{m}\cdot\theta=30m to get \theta=\frac{30\text{m}}{20\text{m}}=1.5rad.It is worth noting here that if we do unit analysis of 20\text{m}/30\text{m}, we see that the units cancel out. Therefore, technically radians are unitless.

statement.p: What is the arc length of one quarter of the circle?

solution.p: The total circumference is 2\pi\cdot20\text{m}=40\pi\text{m}\approx{}125.6637m, so one quarter of the circumference is 40\pi\text{m}/4=10\pi\approx{}31.4159m.

statement.p: What is the radian measure of one quarter of a revolution (the angle for one fourth of a circle)?

solution.p: There are two ways we could approach this. We could use our previous result for the arc length of a quarter circle is approximately 31.4159m and divide by the radius to find the angle, \frac{31.4159\text{m}}{20\text{m}}\approx{}1.57079 or we could realize that there are 2\pi radii in the circumference, and thus a total revolution is 2\pi radians. Then, we get that one quarter of that is \frac{2\pi}{4}=\frac{\pi}{2}\approx{}1.57079 radians.

statement.p: What is the radian measure of one eighth of a revolution?

solution.p: Since there are 2\pi radii in the circumference, and thus a total revolution is 2\pi rad, we get that one eighth of that is \frac{2\pi}{8}=\frac{\pi}{4}\approx{}0.78534 rad.

statement.p: What fraction of the distance around the circle is \frac{\pi}{4}rad?

worksheet.p:
A couple of important things about radians before we move on.
As we noted in the solution to , radians are unitless from a dimensional/unit analysis point of view.
One full revolution, what we are used to thinking of as 360^{\circ}, is 2\pirad. This means that 180^{\circ}=\pi\text{ rad}, and a right angle is 90^{\circ}=\frac{\pi}{2}\text{ rad}. In general, the conversions between degrees and radians are
{d}{\text{ deg}}&=\frac{\pi}{180}d\text{ rad},&\theta\text{ rad}&=\theta{\left(\frac{180}{\pi}\right)}{\text{ deg}}.
Some important angles to become familiar with are:
\frac{\pi}{6}&=30^{\circ}, & \frac{\pi}{4}&=45^{\circ}, & \frac{\pi}{3}&=60^{\circ}, & \frac{\pi}{2}&=90^{\circ},
\frac{2\pi}{3}&=120^{\circ}, & \frac{3\pi}{4}&=135^{\circ}, & \frac{5\pi}{6}&=150^{\circ}, & \pi&=180^{\circ},
\frac{7\pi}{6}&=210^{\circ}, & \frac{5\pi}{4}&=225^{\circ}, & \frac{4\pi}{3}&=240^{\circ}, & \frac{3\pi}{2}&=270^{\circ},
\frac{5\pi}{3}&=300^{\circ}, & \frac{7\pi}{4}&=315^{\circ}, & \frac{11\pi}{6}&=330^{\circ}, & 2\pi&=360^{\circ}.

introduction.p: Probably the two most important functions in trigonometry are defined based on angles and the coordinates of points on a circle of radius 1, which we refer to as the unit circle.

For any point, P, on the unit circle, we measure the angle for P in radians from the positive x-axis counter-clockwise to P. Negative angles and angles greater than 2\pi are allowed: negative angles are measured counter-clockwise from the positive x-axis, and angles greater than 2\pi (or less than -2\pi) start around the circle again.

figure.caption: The Unit Circle with an Angle Shown

description.p: The Unit Circle with an Angle and a Point Shown

introduction.p: shows the unit circle with a point P=(a,b) and its angle, \theta.
Now that we have the unit circle and have explained how we measure angles on the unit circle, we are ready to define the circular functions sine and cosine.

statement.p: For any real number \theta, define the point P=(a,b) on the unit circle whose angle (measured from the positive x-axis) is \thetarad. Then the cosine of \theta is the x-coordinate of P and the sine of \theta is the y-coordinate of P. That is, \cos(\theta)&=a, &\sin(\theta)&=b.
We will find \sin\left(\frac{\pi}{4}\right) and \cos\left(\frac{\pi}{4}\right).

We know that \frac{\pi}{4} is 45^{\circ}, so we start by drawing a point on the unit circle that makes an angle of \frac{\pi}{4} with the positive x-axis and drop a perpendicular from the point to the x-axis.

Because we now have a 45,45,90 triangle, we know the x- and y-coordinates of P will be the same size, and because we are in the first quadrant, they will both be positive. So, let P=(a,a), where a>0, and we will find the value of a, and therefore the sine and cosine of \frac{\pi}{4}.

description.p: The Unit Circle with an Angle, a Point, and a Segment to the x-axis Shown

statement.p: From the Pythagorean theorem, since the unit circle has radius 1 and the radius of the unit circle is the hypotenuse of the right triangle, we have a^{2}+a^{2}=1^{2} so 2a^{2}=1.
Therefore, we now know that \cos\left(\frac{\pi}{4}\right)=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} and \sin\left(\frac{\pi}{4}\right)=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}.

introduction.p: In the following explorations, use symmetry, the Pythagorean theorem, and geometry to relate angles and the values of sine and cosine.

One geometry fact you may not know is the following: in a triangle with angles \frac{\pi}{6}=30^{\circ}, \frac{\pi}{3}=60^{\circ}, and \frac{\pi}{2}=90^{\circ} (a 30-60-90 triangle) , the shortest side (opposite the 30^{\circ}=\frac{\pi}{6} angle) is half the length of the hypotenuse (longest side).

statement.p: Find \sin\left(\frac{\pi}{6}\right) and \cos\left(\frac{\pi}{6}\right).

solution.p: Dropping a perpendicular from the point at \frac{\pi}{6} on the unit circle creates a 30-60-90 triangle with the perpendicular being the shortest side. Since the hypotenuse has length 1, that means that the y-coordinate of the point is \frac{1}{2}, and so \sin\left(\frac{\pi}{6}\right)=\frac{1}{2}. Then, from the Pythagorean theorem, if we let the x-coordinate of the point be a, we have a^{2}+\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{2}=1^{2} so a^{2}+\frac{1}{4}=1 and therefore a^{2}=\frac{3}{4}. Since we know that a>0, we know that a=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}. Thus, \cos\left(\frac{\pi}{6}\right)=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}.

statement.p: Find \sin\left(\frac{\pi}{3}\right) and \cos\left(\frac{\pi}{3}\right).

hint.p: Use symmetry and the previous problem.

statement.p: Find \sin\left(\frac{5\pi}{6}\right) and \cos\left(\frac{5\pi}{6}\right).

solution.p: Dropping a perpendicular from the point at \frac{5\pi}{6} on the unit circle creates a 30-60-90 triangle with the perpendicular being the shortest side. Since the hypotenuse has length 1, that means that the y-coordinate of the point is \frac{1}{2}, and so \sin\left(\frac{5\pi}{6}\right)=\frac{1}{2}. Then, from the Pythagorean theorem, if we let the x-coordinate of the point be a, we have a^{2}+\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{2}=1^{2} so a^{2}+\frac{1}{4}=1 and therefore a^{2}=\frac{3}{4}. Since the point is in the second quadrant, we know that a\lt 0, so we know that a=\frac{-\sqrt{3}}{2}. Thus, \cos\left(\frac{5\pi}{6}\right)=\frac{-\sqrt{3}}{2}.

worksheet.title: Similar Triangles and the Pythagorean Theorem

introduction.p: An extremely important concept in physics, trigonometry, calculus, and even carpentry is the notion of similar triangles. We will briefly discuss how to recognize similar triangles and what properties they have before returning to the ideas we explored in .
Combining the definitions of sine and cosine with similar triangles and the Pythagorean theorem gives us tools that make these functions extremely useful in a variety of situations.

statement.p: When two triangles have exactly the same three angles, we say that they are similar triangles or that the triangles are similar.

description.p: An image of two similar triangles. That is, two triangles of different sizes but with the same angle measurements.

introduction.p: The triangles shown in are similar because angle C is the same as angle D (\angle C\cong \angle D), angle B is the same as angle E (\angle B\cong \angle E), and angle A is the same as angle F (\angle A\cong \angle F).

We say that \angle C and \angle D, \angle B and \angle E, \angle A and \angle F are corresponding angles, and similarly, we say that sides \overline{CB} and \overline{DE}, sides \overline{BA} and \overline{EF}, sides \overline{AC} and \overline{FD} are corresponding sides.
Furthermore, we say that \triangle CBA \sim \triangle DEF, and the order matters!

statement.p: Given two triangles, \triangle MNE and \triangle PQR, when the triangles are similar (\triangle MNE\sim\triangle PQR), the lengths of the corresponding sides are proportional.

introduction.p:
Applying to , for example, we have that \frac{f}{a}=\frac{e}{b}=\frac{d}{c}, and, equivalently,
\frac{a}{c}&=\frac{f}{d},& \frac{a}{b}&=\frac{f}{e},& \frac{b}{c}&=\frac{d}{e}.

statement.p: For any positive numbers, a, b, and c, if a and b are the lengths of two legs of a right triangle and c is the length of the hypoteneuse, then a^{2}+b^{2}=c^{2}.

Furthermore, for any triangle with side lengths a, b, and c, if a^{2}+b^{2}=c^{2}, then the triangle is a right triangle, the sides with lengths a and b are the legs, and the side with length c is the hypotenuse.

introduction.p: In , \overline{OA} has length 0.5m, \overline{OB} has length 1m, and \overline{OD} has length 3m.

statement.p: Explain why \triangle{}OBA is similar to \triangle{}ODC.

solution.p: Both triangles share \angle{}AOB\cong{}\angle{}COD, and \angle{}DCO and \angle{}BAO are both right angles. Because the measures of the three angles of any triangle add to 180^{\circ}=\piradians, we must have \angle{}OBA\cong\angle{}ODC.
Since all three angles of \triangle{}OBA are congruent to the respective angles of \triangle{}ODC, the two triangles are similar, \triangle{}OBA\sim{}\triangle{}ODC.

statement.p: Use the fact that \triangle{}OBA\sim{}\triangle{}ODC to find the length of \overline{OC}.

solution.p: We will represent the length of a segment as the two endpoints, so, for example, we will say that OA=0.5m.
We know that OA=0.5m, OB=1m, and OD=3m.

worksheet.title: Practical Applications of Sine and Cosine

statement.p: We will show how to use sine, cosine, and similar triangles to solve a practical problem.

figure.caption: Two Gatehouses on a Canal Lock

description.p: An image showing a canal lock with a gatehouse on each side.

statement.p: Amir is standing at the edge of a canal lock. There are gatehouses on each side of the lock. The gatehouse on the same side as Amir is located 30m from them. Amir wants to find out how wide the lock is by finding how far one gatehouse is from the other. Amir measures the angle from the near gatehouse to the far gatehouse and finds that it is 0.69474\text{ rad}.
How wide is the lock?

We start by drawing a copy of the unit circle centered on Amir's position, and we will assign the distance between the two gatehouses to the variable d. Then, by dropping a perpendicular from the point, P, where the line from Amir to the far gatehouse crosses the circle, we have similar triangles.

We know that P has coordinates (\cos(0.69474),\sin(0.69474)) (which we will leave unevaluated until the end). Furthermore, we know from similar triangles that corresponding parts are proportional, so we have \frac{d}{\sin(0.69474)}=\frac{30\text{m}}{\cos(0.69474)}.
Inaya wants to use trigonometry to measure the height of a tree. She walks 10m away from the base of the tree and measures the angle to the top of the tree as shown in .
To the nearest tenth of a meter, how tall is the tree? That is, what is the value of d in meters?

description.p: Image of a tree and an observer 10m away.

solution.p: Draw a circle that represents the unit circle around the point representing Inaya and set your coordinate axes so that this is the origin.

Drop a perpendicular from where the circle intersects the line from Inaya to the top of the tree. We then have a small triangle with corners at the origin, on the unit circle, and on the x-axis. This triangle is similar to the triangle from the origin to the top of the tree to the x-axis because the share the angle \theta and they both have right angles on the x-axis.

statement.p: Micah is watching a train as it approaches. He is 10m from the closest point on the track.

Now move the slider for d to -2. How does the transformed graph (red) compare to the original (blue).
How would you describe the effect of d on the graph?

introduction.p: In his book, How To Solve It, mathematician George Polya formulated four steps that apply to any type of problem solving. These steps are Understand the Problem, Make a Plan, Carry Out the Plan, and Look Back.

Sometimes it feels like math classes give almost all their attention to carrying out a plan with little attention paid to the other three steps. Often, instructors give students the plan rather than asking them to work on understanding and formulating a plan for themselves, and almost no time is given to looking back.
This handout gives more information on each of the four steps, and in future problems we will attempt to apply all four.

paragraphs.title: Understanding the Problem
paragraphs.p: First. you have to understand the problem.

What is the unknown? What are the data? What is the condition? Is it possible to satisfy the condition? Is the condition sufficient to determine the unknown? Or is it insufficient? Or redundant? Or contradictory?
Draw a figure. Introduce suitable notation. Separate the various parts of the condition. Can you write them down?

paragraphs.title: Devising a Plan
paragraphs.p: Second. Find the connection between the data and the unknown.
You may be obliged to consider auxiliary problems if an immediate connection cannot be found. You should obtain eventually a plan of the solution.
Have you seen it before? Or have you seen the same problem in a slightly different form?
Do you know a related problem? Do you know a theorem that could be useful? Look at the unknown! And try to think of a familiar problem having the same or a similar unknown.

Here is a problem related to yours and solved before. Could you use it? Could you use its result? Could you use its method? Should you introduce some auxiliary element in order to make its use possible?
Could you restate the problem? Could you restate it still differently? Go back to definitions.

If you cannot solve the proposed problem try to solve first some related problem. Could you imagine a more accessible related problem? A more general problem? A more special problem? An analogous problem? Could you solve a part of the problem? Keep only a part of the condition, drop the other part; how far is the unknown then determined, how can it vary? Could you derive something useful from the data? Could you think of other data appropriate to determine the unknown? Could you change the unknown or the data, or both if necessary, so that the new unknown and the new data are nearer to each other?
Did you use all the data? Did you use the whole condition? Have you taken into account all essential notions involved in the problem?

paragraphs.title: Carrying Out the Plan
paragraphs.p: Third. Carry out your plan.

Carrying out your plan of the solution, check each step. Can you see clearly that the step is correct? Can you prove that it is correct? LOOKING BACK Fourth. Examine the solution obtained. Can you check the result? Can you check the argument? Can you derive the result differently? Can you see it at a glance? Can you use the result, or the method, for some other problem?

paragraphs.title: Looking Back
paragraphs.p: Fourth. Examine the solution obtained.
Can you check the result? Can you check the argument?
Can you derive the result differently? Can you see it at a glance?
Can you use the result, or the method, for some other problem?
